issues.legal_issue: A High Court should not use supervisory jurisdiction to entertain a challenge to a civil court’s ex parte decree when the civil procedure provides a statutory appeal.
material_facts: The trial court passed an ex parte decree in a civil suit.
The defendants had a remedy of appeal to the First Appellate Court against the decree.
One defendant directly challenged the decree under Article 227, and the High Court set it aside.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in entertaining a supervisory revision against the ex parte decree because a statutory appeal was available.
issues.legal_principle: Where proceedings are before a civil court and the Code of Civil Procedure provides an appellate remedy, that remedy ordinarily operates as a near-total bar to supervisory intervention under Article 227. The Court relied on Virudhunagar Hindu Nadargal Dharma Paribalana Sabai v. Tuticorin Educational Society, which applied the principles in Radhey Shyam v. Chhabi Nath and referred to A. Venkatasubbiah Naidu v. S. Chellappan. The defendants could also seek to set aside an ex parte decree under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.civil_court_proceeding: The proceeding was conducted before a civil court.
predicates.ex_parte_decree_challenged: A party challenged a decree entered in that party’s absence.
predicates.statutory_appeal_available: The procedural law provided an appeal to a higher court against the decree.
predicates.supervisory_revision_should_not_be_enter: The High Court should not entertain supervisory review of the decree when the stated conditions apply.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an ex parte decree from a civil court and an appeal is available, supervisory revision should not be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court considering a challenge connected with an ex parte decree must address the trial court’s refusal to excuse delay in seeking to set the decree aside, and must not bypass a refusal that has become final.
material_facts: The defendants applied to set aside the ex parte decree after delays of 1,522 and 2,345 days.
The trial court refused to excuse the delays, finding that sufficient cause had not been shown.
One defendant did not challenge the refusal, which therefore attained finality; the other defendants challenged their refusal, but the High Court did not examine whether it was justified.
The High Court set aside the ex parte decree without deciding the validity of the trial court’s delay rulings and commented on the decree’s merits.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred by setting aside the decree without considering whether the trial court was justified in refusing to excuse the delays; it also could not bypass the unchallenged refusal that had become final.
issues.legal_principle: An application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside an ex parte decree requires consideration of the delay in making the application where delay must be excused. A reviewing court must address the legality of the refusal to excuse delay before setting aside the decree, and cannot use supervisory jurisdiction to circumvent an unchallenged order that has attained finality. The Court also held that the High Court had treated the matter as if it were exercising appellate jurisdiction, without addressing the relevant threshold rulings.

rule.if: civil_court_proceeding and ex_parte_decree_challenged and delay_relief_refused and (refusal_order_unexamined or refusal_order_final_and_unappealed)

predicates.civil_court_proceeding: The underlying proceeding was conducted before a civil court.
predicates.ex_parte_decree_challenged: A party challenged a decree entered in that party’s absence.
predicates.delay_relief_refused: The trial court refused to excuse delay in an application seeking to set aside the decree.
predicates.refusal_order_unexamined: The reviewing court set aside the decree without examining whether the trial court’s refusal to excuse delay was justified.
predicates.refusal_order_final_and_unappealed: A party did not appeal or otherwise challenge the refusal to excuse delay, and that refusal became final.
predicates.supervisory_court_must_not_bypass_delay_: A supervisory court must not set aside the decree while bypassing the trial court’s refusal to excuse delay.

issues.definition: When a civil court has refused to excuse delay in an application concerning an ex parte decree, a supervisory court must not bypass that refusal if it has not been examined or has become final without challenge.
